title: The shine comes back
hookLine: a brass pot polished before a festival gets no new shine; the old one comes back, and Ramanuja says moksha works the same way
carry: moksha: your own shine uncovered, still you, near god

lines: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A SELF IS FREE?
cards: The night before a festival, someone sits on the floor with the family's old brass pot, a lemon, some ash or tamarind, and a cloth. The pot has gone dull and brown. Rub, rinse, rub.
Slowly it glows. Nobody added gold. Nothing new went in.

The shine was the brass all along, under a film of time and smoke. Ramanuja reaches the last part of the Brahma Sutras, where the question is what happens to a self when it's finally free. Does it vanish?
Does it turn into something else? His answer looks a lot like that pot on the floor.

teach.h: MOKSHA: IT APPEARS IN ITS OWN FORM.
teach.b: Moksha, freedom, is the goal so many Hindu paths point to. The Chandogya Upanishad says the freed self, reaching the highest light, appears in its own form.
The Brahma Sutra picks up that phrase, and Ramanuja leans hard on the word own. Freedom isn't the self getting a new nature; it's the self's real nature showing, the way the brass's shine shows.
Its awareness, narrowed by karma, opens fully.
It's free of evil, free of death and grief, with desires that come true, the same marks the Upanishad gave to the highest self. So does the freed self dissolve into God, like a drop into the sea?
The self stays a self. It knows Brahman directly, and experiences itself as inseparable from him, the way a body belongs to its soul. It shares Brahman's joy fully.

But the Brahma Sutra draws one line, and Ramanuja keeps it: the freed self shares in everything except the running of the world. Creating, holding up and dissolving the universe stays with the Lord alone.
Freed selves don't become rival gods. They're near enough to share every joy, and still themselves, still loving. For Sri Vaishnavas, freedom isn't the end of the relationship.

It's the relationship with nothing in the way; they picture it as serving Vishnu forever in his realm, Vaikuntha. Other schools of Vedanta describe freedom differently, and each reads these same sutras with care.

how: Sri Vaishnavas describe liberation, moksha, as the self reaching Vishnu's own realm, Vaikuntha, and serving him there forever in joy; teachers study Ramanuja's comments on the last section of the Brahma Sutras for this teaching.

o: careful thought about Vishnu, selves and freedom
rules for how Vishnu's temples hold their festivals
the family stories of Vishnu's devotees

games.q: the shine comes back: tap the pairs.
p: nothing new, only the old shine

s: for Ramanuja, the freed self dissolves into God like a drop in the sea
the self stays itself, knows Brahman directly and is never apart from him.
the freed self shares everything except running the world
creating and holding up the universe stays with the Lord alone.
Ramanuja says freedom gives the self a brand-new nature
it's the self's own nature uncovered, like brass polished back to its shine.

games.q: you're a freed self in Ramanuja's reading, sharing Brahman's joy completely. what don't you do?
games.why: Ramanuja keeps the Brahma Sutra's line: freed selves share everything except the running of the world.

practice: Bring to mind one good thing in you that's gone dull lately: patience, humor, generosity, attention.

Don't try to make it new; picture the film over it, tiredness, hurry, an old hurt, and on each out-breath let a little of it come away. Notice what was there all along, and if you pray, hold that shine toward the name you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Vaishnava theology. Today, moksha as the self appearing in its own form: uncovered, still itself, near God, sharing every joy except running the world.

orig.note: Sanskrit: in its own form, the Chandogya's phrase for the freed self, central to Ramanuja's reading.

carryVoice: Your line: moksha: your own shine uncovered, still you, near God. Nothing new went in; the shine was there all along. Rest well.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.12.3 (reaching the highest light, it appears in its own form)
Brahma Sutra 4.4.1, 4.4.4 and 4.4.17, with Ramanuja's Sri Bhashya (own form; inseparable; except the running of the world)
Chandogya Upanishad 8.7.1 (free from evil, death and grief; whose desires are real)
